title: Ra and the Destruction of Mankind
subtitle: A rebellion, the divine Eye, and the beer ruse

complaint.author: E. A. Wallis Budge
complaint.locator: Legend of the Destruction of Mankind, Chapter I, human complaint; local text normalized characters 118442-118701
complaint.excerpt: Now men and women were speaking words of complaint, saying:--"Behold, his Majesty (Life, Strength, and Health to him!) hath grown old, and his bones have become like silver, and his members have turned into gold and his hair is like unto real lapis- lazuli."

eye.excerpt: Then the Majesty of Nu, to son Ra, spake, saying:--"Thou art the god who art greater than he who made thee, thou art the sovereign of those who were created with thee, thy throne is set, and the fear of thee is great; let thine Eye go against those who have uttered blasphemies against thee.

beer.work: Legend of the Destruction of Mankind, the beer plan
beer.author: E. A. Wallis Budge
beer.locator: Legend of the Destruction of Mankind, the beer plan; local text normalized characters 122463-123525
beer.excerpt: Now when the Majesty of Re, the King of the South and North, had come with the gods to look at the vessels of beer, and behold, the daylight had appeared after the slaughter of men and women by the goddess in their season as she sailed up the river, the Majesty of Ra said, "It is good, it is good, nevertheless I must protect men and women against her." And Ra, said, "Let them take up the vases and carry them to the place where the men and women were slaughtered by her." Then the Majesty of the King of the South and North in the three-fold beauty of the night caused to be poured out these vases of beer which make [men] to lie down (or, sleep), and the meadows of the Four Heavens[FN#61] were filled with beer (or, water) by reason of the Souls of the Majesty of this god. And it came to pass that when this goddess arrived at the dawn of day, she found these [Heavens] flooded [with beer], and she was pleased thereat; and she drank [of the beer and blood], and her heart rejoiced, and she became drunk, and she gave no further attention to men and women.
beer.note: Verbatim translation excerpt; whitespace normalized. Keep the ancient text separate from Budge's editorial notes.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: In this translated legend, people complain that Ra has grown old. He consults the gods, and the divine Eye is sent against the rebels. Later, beer mixed with mandrake and blood makes the goddess drink and stop the slaughter.

narrativeBlocks.title: Humans complain and Ra consults
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Budge translation; whitespace normalized): “Now men and women were speaking words of complaint, saying:--"Behold, his Majesty (Life, Strength, and Health to him!) hath grown old, and his bones have become like silver, and his members have turned into gold and his hair is like unto real lapis- lazuli."”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The tale connects royal authority, rebellion, violence, and a ruse that ends the slaughter. Preserve the episode's sequence rather than simplifying it to 'Ra brings order.'

narrativeBlocks.title: Read the evidence carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Budge presents this as a translated Egyptian legend with editorial framing. The passage is one literary account, not proof that every Egyptian community held a single creation or order doctrine.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: Compare the decision to release the Eye with the later beer plan. The story gives two different moments of divine action.
